extractor.prompt: Extract inheritance engagements: where Husserl engages predecessors on intentionality and descriptive psychology in Husserliana 9 editors' introduction
extractor.note: Partial pass focused on sections d-e presenting Husserl's engagements with Brentano (doctrine of intentionality, differences on methodology) and Dilthey (descriptive-analytic psychology).

coverage_note: Covers sections d-e: historical engagement with Brentano's discovery of intentionality and Husserl's methodological departures; positioning vis-à-vis empirical and eidetic approaches. Not covered: engagement with Leibniz-Wolff school, Kant's critique, or section f on transcendental extension.

predecessor.author: Brentano
predecessor.text: Doctrine of intentionality as fundamental character of consciousness

engagements.claim: Husserl credits Brentano with discovering intentionality as the fundamental character of consciousness through inner experience, establishing it as the basis for descriptive psychology.
engagements.quote: Husserl thus crowns Brentano with the historical achievement of *intentionality as the fundamental character of consciousness*.

engagements.claim: Brentano opened the path but did not work out the methodology of intentional analysis; Husserl's task was to complete what Brentano left undone.
engagements.quote: Brentano *opened* the path but did not work out the methodology of intentional analysis; what remained was for Husserl to do this.

engagements.claim: Husserl recognizes Dilthey's demand for purely descriptive psychology as a foundational discipline for the human sciences, and identifies convergence between his phenomenology and Dilthey's program.
engagements.quote: the *Logical Investigations*, although they had arisen outside all relation to his writings, with great joy and saw in them a *first concrete execution* of his "Ideas Concerning a Descriptive and Analytic Psychology."

predecessor.author: Dilthey
predecessor.text: Psychology and philosophical method in the Geisteswissenschaften

engagements.claim: Husserl later recognized that Dilthey's writings contain an inspired pre-view and pre-stage of phenomenology, offering valuable concrete stimuli for phenomenological work despite lack of strict methodological form.
engagements.quote: His writings contain an inspired *pre-view* and *pre-stage* of phenomenology. They are by no means antiquated; even today they remain overrich in most valuable concrete stimuli for work in the methodologically advanced and, in its whole problematic, differently shaped phenomenology.

predecessor.author: Brentano
predecessor.text: Conceptual naturalism in treatment of psychology

engagements.claim: Husserl identifies Brentano as still operating within naturalistic assumptions about consciousness, failing to recognize intentional implication and analysis as distinct from physical combination.
engagements.quote: Even Brentano was, in the indicated sense, a naturalist: something like *intentional implication* and *intentional analysis* as the analysis of possibly continuously-into-one-another-wound sense-givings he had not yet seen.

engagements.claim: Brentano's approach remained externally classificatory-descriptive; the Logical Investigations advanced beyond this by asking how possible modes of consciousness correlate with objective categories.
engagements.quote: Brentano had not gone beyond an externally classificatory-descriptive consideration of intentional experiences — or, what is the same, of *modes of consciousness*.
